title: Ignatius of Antioch
lead: Ignatius, overseer of the church at Antioch in Syria, was taken under guard to Rome to die by wild beasts; Jerome says he 'was put to death the eleventh year of Trajan' (Lives of Illustrious Men 16). He opens his letter to Polycarp as 'Ignatius, who is also called Theophorus'. On the way he wrote seven letters to churches of Asia, to Rome and to Polycarp. They are in no church's Bible. The works list calls them the Letters of Ignatius. Three of them are translated on this site: Ignatius to the Ephesians, Ignatius to the Romans and Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans.

sections.b: Eusebius says Ignatius was 'chosen bishop of Antioch, second in succession to Peter', was 'sent from Syria to Rome' and 'became food for wild beasts on account of his testimony to Christ'. He wrote from Smyrna to the Ephesians, Magnesians, Trallians and Romans, and from Troas to the Philadelphians, the Smyrnaeans and Polycarp (Church History 3.36.2-10, NPNF). Polycarp sent copies of the letters he had to the Philippians (Polycarp to the Philippians 13:2), whose wish 'to make a collection of the letters of Ignatius', Lake says, called his own letter forth.
sections.refs: Polycarp to the Philippians 9:1; Polycarp to the Philippians 13:1-2; Acts 11:26

sections.b: The site translates three of the seven letters from Lake's Greek of the short recension. Ignatius to the Ephesians, written from Smyrna, thanks the church that sent its overseer Onesimus to meet him and sets out the letters' great themes: unity with the overseer, Christ 'God in man', and the one bread, 'the medicine of immortality'. Ignatius to the Romans, also from Smyrna, asks the Roman Christians not to save him from the beasts: 'I am God's wheat'. Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans, from Troas, argues against those who said Christ suffered only in appearance, and has 'the catholic church' (8:2), which the Catholic Encyclopedia (1910) and a district calendar of the Lutheran Church—Missouri Synod call the first use of the phrase. The other four, To the Magnesians, To the Trallians, To the Philadelphians and To Polycarp, are named in the works list.
